title: Size the catalogue import's maps for the batch

blocks.text: The catalogue import loads one batch of SKUs at a time, and the batch header says how many rows follow. A profile of an import shows time in `HashMap.resize` and `ConcurrentHashMap.transfer` on every batch, and a heap dump shows the stock cache's table twice the length of the price index's, for the same number of SKUs.
`CatalogMaps` builds three maps per batch. Finish its three factory methods in `src/main/java/practice/CatalogMaps.java`:

items: `newPriceIndex(skus)`: filled once by the import thread, then only read;
`newRecentTable(maxEntries)`: the table behind `RecentLookups`, a cache of the prices users looked up most recently, which drops the one used least recently when it is full.

blocks.text: When you're done, none of the three grows its table while a batch loads or while the cache evicts, and the stock cache's table is no longer than it needs to be. About three lines in total.
The tests read each map's table length by reflection.

cases.says: the price index holds every row of a batch
the stock cache holds every row of a batch
the recent-lookups cache keeps at most its limit of entries, the newest ones when nothing is read
the price index takes a whole batch without growing its table
the stock cache takes a whole batch without growing its table
the stock cache's table is the smallest that holds the batch
an entry read recently survives the next eviction, and the one nobody read goes
the recent-lookups cache never grows its table, while it fills or while it evicts

origin.section: ConcurrentHashMap Is Sized in Entries, and Its Load Factor Only Sizes the First Table

concepts: An access-ordered LinkedHashMap needs the three-argument constructor, whose int is a bucket count; LinkedHashMap.newLinkedHashMap(n) gives insertion order.
ConcurrentHashMap's constructor takes a number of entries, so passing it the HashMap formula doubles its table for some counts.
A ConcurrentHashMap's load factor argument only sizes its first table; every resize comes when the size reaches three-quarters of the table.

The int that HashMap's, HashSet's and LinkedHashMap's constructors take is a bucket count rounded up to a power of two, and the table doubles once the size goes above capacity x load factor, so new HashMap<>(n) resizes before n entries for many n; HashMap.newHashMap(n) takes the entry count.
